summary: Defines a way to split packets across several parallel PPP links, number the pieces, and put them back in order at the other end. This lets a host combine multiple slower links, such as several dial-up lines, into one larger logical connection.

plainLanguage.summary: PPP Multilink combines several links between two systems into one logical link. It numbers packet fragments so the receiving system can restore their order.

questions: how to combine multiple ppp links
what is the endpoint discriminator in ppp

how does ppp combine multiple links
subtitle: PPP splits packets across several links and reassembles them in sequence.

tldr.problem: Several PPP links between the same systems can provide more capacity, but sending packets over them independently can reorder fragments.
tldr.mechanism: The peers negotiate a bundle and add beginning, ending, and sequence information to fragments so the receiver can reassemble packets.
tldr.outcome: Multiple physical links operate as one logical link. RFC 1990 obsoletes RFC 1717 and is a Draft Standard.

today: RFC 1990 is a Draft Standard published in August 1996. It obsoletes RFC 1717.

sections.title: Why Combine PPP Links
sections.content:
ISDN and other services can provide several simultaneous channels between two systems. Using multiple links can increase available bandwidth or provide an additional link when needed.

Simply alternating packets across links can reorder them because links may have different delays. PPP Multilink adds sequencing and synchronization information so the receiver can rebuild packets in order.
sections.plainLanguage: Several links can carry data between the same systems. Multilink adds sequence information because the links may deliver their parts at different times.

sections.title: The Bundle as a Virtual Link
sections.content:
Each physical link first uses normal PPP procedures, including LCP configuration and any authentication. Multilink then treats links between the same two systems as one aggregate link, called a bundle.

The bundle acts as a virtual PPP link with its own Multilink Protocol. Packets without Multilink headers cannot be sequenced, so they may be delivered in any convenient order.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers configure each physical link, then group selected links into a bundle. Network protocols can use that bundle as one logical PPP link.

sections.title: Fragment Header and Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
A packet is encapsulated using PPP rules and divided into fragments sized for member links. Each fragment uses protocol identifier 0x00-0x3d and a Multilink header. Small packets need not be fragmented, and fragments need not have equal sizes.

The default header has a Beginning bit, an Ending bit, reserved bits, and a 24-bit sequence number. Negotiation can select a shorter 12-bit sequence number. The sequence number increases for every fragment, including a fragment containing a complete packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Each fragment says whether it begins or ends a packet and carries a sequence number. The receiver uses those fields to put the packet back together.

sections.title: Negotiating Bundle Options
sections.content:
The Multilink MRRU option indicates Multilink support and the largest reassembled Information field the peer accepts. A system MUST be able to receive 1500 octets. The peers must negotiate the option before sending Multilink packets.

The Short Sequence Number option requests 12-bit sequence numbers; without it, sequence numbers are 24 bits. The Endpoint Discriminator identifies a system so a newly established link can be matched to an existing bundle. Authentication is needed to stop a hostile peer from joining by presenting a false discriminator.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers agree on the maximum reassembled packet size and sequence format. An endpoint identifier helps them decide whether a new link belongs in an existing bundle.

sections.title: Detecting Missing Fragments
sections.content:
The sender uses strictly increasing sequence numbers on each member link. The receiver tracks the latest sequence number from every link and maintains their minimum. When that minimum moves beyond the ending fragment of an incomplete packet, the receiver can treat the missing fragment as lost.

An idle link can delay loss detection because its sequence number does not advance. Senders SHOULD avoid idle member links; a null fragment may advance a link without payload. The RFC does not prescribe a link-failure detection method.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver compares progress across all links. If every link has moved beyond a missing fragment, it can discard the incomplete packet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says Multilink is no more and no less secure than the PPP authentication protocols. The Endpoint Discriminator alone is not proof of identity: a hostile peer could falsify it to try to join a bundle.

PPP authentication can provide the authenticated peer information needed when deciding whether links belong to the same system.
sections.plainLanguage: The bundle is only as trustworthy as the peer authentication. A discriminator by itself can be copied or falsified.
